# DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies

**Authors:** Haichuan Wang Affiliation: Harvard University Email: haichuanwang@g.harvard.edu Anagha Satish Affiliation: Harvard University Jiale Zheng Affiliation: Harvard University Saisneha Ghatti Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Lingkai Kong Affiliation: Harvard University Kai Wang Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Milind Tambe Affiliation: Harvard University

## Abstract

Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies’ Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

## 1 Introduction

In real-world decision making, many choices are strategic: a party’s outcome depends not only on its own decisions, but also on those of adversaries with competing objectives. Game theory provides a framework for modeling these interactions. In many applications, however, strategic decisions are not naturally enumerable and instead lie in continuous action spaces (Stein et al., 2008; Ganzfried, 2021; Kroer and Sandholm, 2015). In spatial security games, for example, a defender allocates resources while an adversary chooses where to attack (Kamra et al., 2018; Gan et al., 2017; Alpern et al., 2022); these decisions are naturally represented by locations or trajectories rather than discrete actions. Continuous decisions also arise in economic competition, where firms choose production quantities (Shi and Zhang, 2020), and in resource-allocation games, where players divide continuous budgets across competing objectives (Roberson, 2006). Such settings are difficult to capture with finite strategy spaces and require reasoning over distributions on large continuous action spaces.

A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile in which neither player can improve its outcome by unilaterally changing its strategy. A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over a player’s possible actions; in continuous games, this distribution may be defined over an infinite action space (Glicksberg, 1952). As the dimensionality and complexity of the action space grow, representing the mixed strategy itself becomes challenging, since equilibrium play may require complex, multimodal distributions over high-dimensional continuous actions (Perkins et al., 2015).

Continuous-action games, even in the more well-understood two player zero-sum (2p0s) setting, present unique computation challenges. While efficient algorithms (Dantzig, 1951) and practical solvers (Jain et al., 2011; Cerny et al., 2024) exists for 2p0s games with finite action set, they cannot directly handle infinitely many actions in continuous-action games. Therefore, prior works (Kamra et al., 2019; Martin and Sandholm, 2023) parameterize player strategies with neural networks and optimizes them through iterative algorithms such as Fictitious Play (FP) or Online Mirror Descent (OMD) to approximate Nash equilibria. However, these neural policies can suffer from mode collapse in high-dimensional action spaces, failing to capture the multimodal distributions that naturally arise in continuous-action games. Since diffusion model is capable of modeling multimodality in continuous vectors (Ho et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024), we ask

Can we parameterize player strategy with diffusion policies in iterative game-solving algorithms?

In this work we propose DiffNash, a method for introducing diffusion models into equilibrium computation for games with continuous action. We parameterize each player’s mixed strategy with a diffusion model and use Online Mirror Descent (OMD) Blair (1985) to iteratively update these strategies towards equilibrium. At each iteration, we sample candidate actions from the player’s current diffusion policy and evaluate how useful those actions would be against the opponent’s current policy. Standard diffusion training assumes access to samples from the target distribution, while the OMD update defines this distribution only implicitly. Hence, we adapt the reweighting technique of Ma et al. (2025) to modify the diffusion training loss, provably recovering the correct target update. To reduce the cost of repeatedly sampling news actions from diffusion and stabilize training along OMD iterations, we reuse samples from past policies through a replay buffer. We correct the resulting distribution shift with importance weighting and approximate the importance weights using Evidence Lower Bounds (ELBOs).

Our main contributions are: (1) We develop a diffusion-policy framework for equilibrium computation in continuous action games using utility-weighted score matching to represent complex, potentially multimodal mixed strategies (Section 3.1) (2) We incorporate a diffusion update into OMD, with an empirical comparison showing substantially faster convergence than a corresponding diffusion-FP approach (Section 3.2) (3) We construct an ELBO-difference based importance weighting that allows past actions to be reused for opponent evaluation (Section 3.3) and stabilizing training (Section 3.4) (4) We evaluate our approach on two continuous-action games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning (Section 5).

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Problem Formulation

We consider a two-player normal-form game $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{A}^{1},\mathcal{A}^{2},u^{1},u^{2})$ , where $\mathcal{A}^{i}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d^{i}}$ is a non-empty compact action space of player $i$ and $u^{i}:\mathcal{A}^{1}\times\mathcal{A}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be its bounded and measurable utility function 11 1 We use superscripts for game-theoretic notation, such as player and equilibrium-solver iteration indices, and subscripts for diffusion model notation.. We consider high-dimensional continuous action set, which may also subject to global feasibility constraints, such as a fixed resource budget or a bounded spatial domain. A mixed strategy $\pi^{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{i})$ is a probability distribution over $\mathcal{A}^{i}$ . Given a strategy profile $\pi=(\pi^{1},\pi^{2})$ , the expected payoff to player 1 is $U^{i}(\pi^{1},\pi^{2})=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}^{1}\sim\pi^{1}\\ \mathbf{a}^{2}\sim\pi^{2}\end{subarray}}\left[u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})\right]$ . Our goal is to find the Nash equilibrium of the game, where neither player has the incentive to deviate from their chosen strategy. Formally,

#### Definition 1 (Nash Equilibrium).

$\pi^{\star}=(\pi^{1,\star},\pi^{2,\star})$ is a Nash equilibrium if, for $i\in\{1,2\}$ , $U^{i}(\pi^{i,\star},\pi^{-i,\star})\geq U^{i}(\pi^{i},\pi^{-i,\star})\qquad\text{for all }\pi^{i}\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{i}).$

We focus primarily on two-player zero-sum (2p0s) games, where $u^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})=-u^{2}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})$ . 2p0s games with finite action can be solved by linear programming (Dantzig, 1951). For games with large combinatorial action spaces, such as network security games, practical methods exploit problem structure and propose practical solvers (Jain et al., 2011; Cerny et al., 2024). Continuous-action games require representing and optimizing distributions over an infinite action space. Recent approaches therefore use neural parameterizations of mixed strategies within iterative game-solving algorithms (Kamra et al., 2019; Martin and Sandholm, 2023). Our work follows this latter setting, using diffusion models as expressive representations of continuous mixed strategies.

We primarily study the 2p0s setting, where equilibrium objective and associated learning dynamics are well understood. Methods with strong convergence guarantees in 2p0s games are also commonly studied and applied in general-sum settings, although convergence to Nash equilibrium is no longer guaranteed (Anagnostides et al., 2022). We also include general-sum games, where player’s objectives are not necessarily opposed and equilibrium computation is generally more challenging. We measure solution quality using the Nash gap, defined as the total improvement available to players through unilateral best responses (Lanctot et al., 2017). It is non-negative and equals zero at Nash equilibrium, measuring how exploitable the strategy profile is.

#### Definition 2 (Nash Gap).

$\operatorname{Gap}(\pi_{1},\pi_{2})=\max_{\pi_{1}^{\prime}\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{1})}U(\pi_{1}^{\prime},\pi_{2})-\min_{\pi_{2}^{\prime}\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{2})}U(\pi_{1},\pi_{2}^{\prime}).$

A low Nash gap limits gains from opponent’s unilateral deviations. We seek such strategies in high-dimensional action spaces, where conventional neural policies struggle (Kamra et al., 2019).

### 2.2 Diffusion Models

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020) is a generative model consisting of two stochastic processes: one forward process which progressively adds noise to the data, and a reverse (denoising) process which learns to gradually remove noise. Formally, given a clean data from the target distribution $\mathbf{z}_{0}\sim p_{0}$ , the forward process gradually perturbs the data by $q(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\,\beta_{t}\mathbf{I}\right)$ , where $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ is the perturbed data at time $t$ and $\beta_{t}$ is the noise variance at time step $t=1,\cdots,T$ . The corresponding joint distribution of forward trajectory is $q_{0:T}(\mathbf{z}_{0:T})=p_{0}(\mathbf{z}_{0})\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t|t-1}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{t-1})$ . Since each step adds independent Gaussian noise, we can sample $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ by $\mathbf{z}_{t}\sim p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})=\int p_{0}(\mathbf{z}_{0})\,q_{t\mid 0}(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{0})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{0}$ , where $q_{t\mid 0}(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{0}):=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{z}_{t};\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{z}_{0},\,(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\mathbf{I}\right),\ \bar{\alpha}_{t}:=\prod_{\ell=1}^{t}\alpha_{\ell},\ \alpha_{t}:=1-\beta_{t}$ . 22 2 Both $p$ and $q$ are density function. We use $q$ to denote tractable distributions like Gaussian corruption. When there is no ambiguity, we use $p$ and $p_{0}$ interchangably.

The backward process recovers the data distribution from a noise distribution $p_{T}$ with a iterative process. When $\beta_{t}$ is small, one can approximate the denoising process by the score function $s(\mathbf{z}_{t}):=\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p(\mathbf{z}_{t})$ . Specifically, $q(\mathbf{z}_{t-1}|\mathbf{z}_{t})\approx N(\mathbf{z}_{t-1};\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}(x_{t}+\beta_{t}s(x_{t})),\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I})$ , where $\sigma_{t}=\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha_{t}}}\beta_{t}$ . Therefore, one can follow the following iterative procedure to draw samples from $p_{0}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{t-1}=\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}(\mathbf{z}_{t}+\beta_{t}s(\mathbf{z}_{t}))+\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\beta_{t}\epsilon_{t} $$

for $t$ from $T$ to $1$ and $\epsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ . However, we do not know $s(\mathbf{z}_{t})$ in closed form, so we train a score network $s_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)$ to approximate it, with the following tractable loss function (Ho et al., 2020):

$$ \displaystyle L(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t\in[T]}(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}_{0}\sim p_{0},\mathbf{z}_{t}\sim q_{t|0}}[||s_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t};t)-\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log q_{t|0}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{z}_{0})||^{2}] $$

Ma et al. (2025) shows that fix a time $t$ , Equation 3 has the same global minimizer as Equation 2:

$$ \displaystyle L(\theta;t)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}_{t}\sim p_{t}}[||s_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t};t)-\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})] $$

Though Equation 3 is intractable because we do not know $\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{z}_{t})$ , it’s important for the reweighting technique used in Section 3.1.

### 2.3 Equilibrium Solvers: Online Mirror Descent and Fictitious Play

Let $u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i};\pi^{-i}):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}^{-i}\sim\pi^{-i}}[u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i},\mathbf{a}^{-i})]$ denote player $i$ ’s expected utility for action $\mathbf{a}^{i}$ against opponent strategy $\pi^{-i}$ . We introduce two major iterative algorithms used to compute Nash equilibrium for continuous action in ML literature: Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP).

Online mirror descent. In OMD (Kivinen and Warmuth, 1997; Beck and Teboulle, 2003), each player computes a KL-regularized best response to the opponent’s strategy from the previous iteration. At iteration $k$ , player i computes

$$ \displaystyle\pi^{i,k+1}(\mathbf{a}^{i})=\pi^{i,k}(\mathbf{a}^{i})\exp(\frac{1}{\eta} u_i(\ownaction;\pi^{-i,k}))/Z_{\mathbf{OMD}}^{i,k}\ , $$

where $\frac{1}{\eta}$ is called temperature and $Z_{\mathbf{OMD}}^{i,k}=\int_{\mathcal{A}^{i}}\pi^{i,k}(\mathbf{a}^{i})\exp\!\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\,u_{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i};\pi^{-i,k})\right)\,da^{i}$ is an intractable unknown constant. We define empirical average of OMD responses as $\Pi^{i,k}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{h=1}^{k}\pi_{\mathbf{OMD}}^{i,h}$ . Under standard regularity conditions and an appropriate learning rate schedule, OMD is a no-regret algorithm on continuous action space (Krichene et al., 2015). When both players play such algorithms, their empirical strategies converge asymptotically to the Nash equilibrium set (Balandat et al., 2016).

Fictitious play. While in OMD player computes a KL-regularized best response to the opponent’s current strategy, in FP (Brown, 1951) player best responds to the empirical distribution of the opponent’s past play (Brown, 1951). FP is known to converge to Nash equilibrium with continuous action space and continuous utility function (Danskin, 1954). We consider a special variant called Generalised Weakened Fictitious Play (GWFP) (Leslie and Collins, 2006). Let $\pi_{\mathbf{GWFP}}^{i,k}$ denote player $i$ ’s best response at iteration $k$ , and let $\Pi^{i,k}:=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{h=1}^{k}\pi_{\mathbf{GWFP}}^{i,h}$ denote the empirical average of its past responses. Under GWFP, player $i$ computes

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{\mathbf{GWFP}}^{i,k+1}=\exp\left(\frac{1}{\eta^{k}}u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i},\Pi^{-i,k})\right)/{Z^{i,k}}\ , $$

where $\eta^{k}$ is called temperature and $Z^{i,k}=\int_{\mathcal{A}^{i}}\exp\left(\frac{u^{i}(a^{i},\Pi^{-i,k})}{\eta_{k}}\right)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}^{i}$ is an intractable normalization constant. Under vanishing temperature condition, $(\Pi^{1,k},\Pi^{2,k})$ converges to the set of Nash equilibria asymptotically under GWFP (Leslie and Collins, 2006).

To represent multimodal mixed strategies, we represent player $i$ ’s latent action with a diffusion model $p_{\theta^{i}}$ . A game-specific map $f^{\mathcal{G}}$ will convert the latent sample to a feasible player action, i.e., $\mathbf{a}^{i}=f^{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{z}),\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\theta^{i}}$ . The resulting mixed strategy is then $\pi_{\theta^{i}}=f_{\#}^{\mathcal{G}}p_{\theta^{i}}$ . We call $\pi_{\theta^{i}}$ player $i$ ’s diffusion policy following Ma et al. (2025)’s notation, abstracting away latent space details.

Understanding Convergence Dynamics. Computing the Nash gap requires solving an intractable best response problem, and approximating it at every iteration is prohibitively expensive. To study convergence dynamics, we use a multi-market Cournot game (Kamra et al., 2019) whose unique Nash equilibrium is an analytically derivable singleton, which we denote as $(\mathbf{a}^{1,*},\mathbf{a}^{2,*})$ . In Cournot game, two firms compete by choosing production level across $d$ independent markets to maximizes total profits. We defer Cournot game’s details to Appendix D.2. We define the distance of a strategy profile $\Pi$ to the equilibrium by $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}\mathbb{E}_{a^{i}\sim\pi^{i}}||a^{i}-a^{i,\star}||_{2}.$ Because this distance is easy to calculate, we compute it at each iteration in the Cournot game to study convergence dynamics.

## 3 Proposed Method

*Figure 1: Overview of DiffNash. Each player samples actions from a diffusion policy into a replay buffer. Both lanes pass through a shared replay weight, obtained from a single-call ELBO difference (Proposition 2), and scored against the opponent’s buffered actions by importance sampling. The OMD weight then reweights the denoising loss. Player $-i$ is updated symmetrically.*

### 3.1 Enabling Diffusion-based GWFP and OMD via Reweighted Score Matching

The game-solving updates in GWFP Equation 5 and OMD Equation 4 both involve unknown normalization constants. Such unnormalized distributions can be viewed as energy-based models, which are generally difficult to train and sample from (Song and Kingma, 2021). Moreover, standard diffusion training requires samples from the target distribution, which are not directly available for the GWFP and OMD updates. Ma et al. (2025) show that, instead of integrating the squared score loss in Equation 3 with respect to $p_{t}$ , the objective can be reweighted by any strictly positive function $g(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ without changing its global minimizer:

$$ \displaystyle L(\theta;t)=\int g(\mathbf{a}_{t})||s_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{t};t)-\nabla_{\mathbf{a}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{a}_{t})||^{2}d\mathbf{a}_{t} $$

By choosing appropriate $g(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ , they derive tractable loss to learn the score function of diffusion policy in online RL. We use $\pi_{t,\mathrm{solver}}^{i,k+1}(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ to denote noise-corrupted target update at time $t$ , i.e., $\pi_{t,\mathrm{solver}}^{i,k+1}(\mathbf{a}_{t}):=\int\pi_{\mathrm{solver}}^{i,k+1}(\mathbf{a}_{0})\,q_{t\mid 0}(\mathbf{a}_{t}\mid\mathbf{a}_{0})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}_{0}$ , where $\mathrm{solver}\in\{\mathrm{GWFP},\mathrm{OMD}\}$ . We adapt the reweighting technique to our setting by setting $p_{t}=\pi_{t,\mathrm{solver}}^{i,k+1}$ and choosing proper $g(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ , so that the resulting objectives can recover score functions of noise-corrupted updated in OMD and GWFP.

#### Proposition 1 (OMD and GWFP Loss).

By choosing an appropriate $g_{\mathrm{OMD}}(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ and substitute it into Equation 6, we can equivalently write their loss functions as

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OMD}}(\theta;t)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}_{0}\sim\pi^{i,k}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}_{t}\sim q_{t|0}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{a}_{0})}\left[\exp\left(\frac{1}{\eta}u^{i}(\mathbf{a}_{0};\pi^{-i,k})\right)\left\|s_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{t},t)-\nabla_{\mathbf{a}_{t}}\log q_{t|0}(\mathbf{a}_{t}\mid\mathbf{a}_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\right]. $$

For every $t\in(0,T]$ , the minimizer of Equation 7 over $s$ is the score function of $\pi^{i,k+1}_{t,\mathrm{OMD}}(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ . In Appendix E.1, we show with a proper $g_{\mathrm{GWFP}}(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ , we can recover the score function of $\pi^{i,k+1}_{t,\mathrm{GWFP}}(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ .

We defer Proposition 1’s proof to Appendix E.1. The intuition of choosing $g({\mathbf{a}_{t}})$ is to ensure we can sample from all distributions appear in the resulting loss. For example, at iteration $k+1$ , we have sampling access to $\pi^{i,k}$ and $q_{t|0}$ , while $u^{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}_{0};\pi^{-i,k})$ can be unbiasedly estimated with samples from opponent’s current strategy $\pi^{-i,k}$ . Thus, the objectives in Proposition 1 are tractable, and optimizing them recover the corresponding score function $\nabla_{\mathbf{a}_{t}}\log\pi_{t,\mathrm{solver}}^{i,k+1}(\mathbf{a}_{t})$ . Recall we only need the score function to perform the iterative diffusion sampling process specified in Equation 1. Hence, these objectives suffice to implement diffusion-based OMD and GWFP updates.

### 3.2 Comparison Between FP and OMD

*Figure 2: We run diffusion-based GWFP and OMD on the Cournot game for $600$ iterations across three random seeds and report their mean distances to the Nash equilibrium.*

In this section, we examine the complementary strengths of FP and OMD to guide the design of an algorithm that combines their advantages. (Perolat et al., 2021; Lauriere et al., 2022) report faster convergence for OMD, partly because best responding to stale historical strategies can slow FP’s convergence. We confirm this finding in Figure 2: we run diffusion-based GWFP and OMD for $600$ iterations on the Cournot game. OMD converges substantially faster in both dimensionalities. With action dimension $d=30$ , GWFP’s distance to equilibrium decreases only marginally, highlighting the difficulty of convergence in high-dimensional action spaces. While prior works are often based on FP Kamra et al. (2019); Karthikeyan and Pant (2025), this result motivates using OMD as our equilibrium solver’s backbone.

Evaluating $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OMD}}(\theta;t)$ in Equation 7 requires estimating the expected utility against the current opponent policy. Using $L$ freshly generated opponent actions, this expectation can be estimated as $\widehat{u}^{i}(\mathbf{a}_{0};\pi^{-i,k})=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}u^{i}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{0},\mathbf{a}_{(\ell)}^{-i,k}\right),\mathbf{a}_{(\ell)}^{-i,k}\sim\pi^{-i,k}.$ However, since diffusion generation involves an iterative denoising process, repeatedly sampling fresh actions from the current opponent policy can be computationally expensive. FP largely avoids this cost because each player best-responds to the opponent’s historical mixture $\Pi^{-i,k}$ . Following Kamra et al. (2019), samples from this mixture can be maintained in a replay buffer, making them cheap to reuse. To improve the sample efficiency of our OMD solver, we similarly maintain a replay buffer for each player and use importance sampling (IS) to correct the distribution shift between the policy that generates a sample and $\pi^{-i,k}$ . Formally, let $k^{(\ell)}$ denote the iteration at which the $\ell$ -th sampled action was generated, so that $\mathbf{a}_{(\ell)}^{-i,k^{(\ell)}}\sim\pi^{-i,k^{(\ell)}}$ . We then have

$$ \widehat{u}^{i}(\mathbf{a}_{0};\pi^{-i,k})=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}r^{-i,k,k^{(\ell)}}u^{i}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{0},\mathbf{a}_{(\ell)}^{-i,k^{(\ell)}}\right),\ \text{where }r^{-i,k,k^{(\ell)}}=\frac{\pi_{\theta^{-i,k}}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{(\ell)}^{-i,k^{(\ell)}}\right)}{\pi_{\theta^{-i,k_{\ell}}}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{(\ell)}^{-i,k^{(\ell)}}\right),} $$

$r^{-i,k,k^{(\ell)}}$ is sample $l$ ’s importance weight33 3 In practice, we use $\min\left\{r^{-i,k,k^{(\ell)}},C\right\}$ as the weight in Equation 8, where $C$ caps the weight to prevent excessively large values (Schulman et al., 2017).. However, computing $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot)$ in $r^{-i,k,k^{(\ell)}}$ exactly remains expensive for diffusion models (Song et al., 2020), motivating us to develop a principled proxy.

### 3.3 Enable Importance Sampling

In this section, we fix a player and suppress the player index. Consider a diffusion sample $\mathbf{a}_{0}$ .

#### Lemma 1.

$r^{k,k^{(\ell)}}=\exp\left(\log\pi_{\theta^{k}}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{0})\right)-\log\pi_{\theta^{k^{(\ell)}}}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_{0}\right)\right)$ .

Lemma 1 is proved by direct calculation. By Lemma 1, we only need to approximate $\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0})$ to enable efficient importance sampling. We achieve this by using evidence lower bounds (ELBO).

#### Definition 3.

The ELBO of a sample $\mathbf{a}_{0}$ is $\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{q(\mathbf{a}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{a}_{0})}\left[\log\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0:T})}{q(\mathbf{a}_{1:T}\mid\mathbf{a}_{0})}\right]$ .

ELBO lower bounds the log-likelihood, i.e., $\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0})\leq\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0})$ (Ho et al., 2020). Since $\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0})$ is intractable for diffusion, the ELBO is commonly used as a tractable surrogate for training diffusion models. McAllister et al. (2026) also uses ELBO to approximate IS weight, though their method is for flow matching policy. We develop new method for diffusion policy. Substituting log likelihood with ELBO in Lemma 1, it remains to compute $\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta^{k}}(\mathbf{a}_{0})-\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta^{k^{(\ell)}}}(\mathbf{a}_{0})$ to obtain IS weights. Although evaluating each ELBO is still expensive (Ho et al., 2020), Proposition 2 shows that their difference admits an unbiased estimator requiring only one score network evaluation.

#### Proposition 2.

Suppose $\pi^{k^{(\ell)}}$ and $\pi^{k}$ share the same forward-noising schedule $\{\beta_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ . Denote $D(\theta;\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)=C_{t}||s_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{t},t)+\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}||_{2}^{2}$ , where $C_{t}$ a constant and $\mathbf{a}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{a}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha_{t}}}\epsilon$ . If $t\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T\}$ and $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ , then $\widehat{\Delta}^{k,k^{(\ell)}}:=T\bigl(D(\theta^{k^{(\ell)}};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)-D(\theta^{k};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)\bigr)$ is ELBO difference’s unbiased estimator: $\mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon}[\widehat{\Delta}^{k,k^{(\ell)}}]=\operatorname{ELBO}^{k}(\mathbf{a}_{0})-\operatorname{ELBO}^{k^{(\ell)}}(\mathbf{a}_{0}).$

The proof is deferred to Section E.2. In iteration $k^{(\ell)}$ , when we sample $\mathbf{a}_{0}\sim\pi^{k^{(\ell)}}$ , we record $\left[\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon,D(\theta^{k^{(\ell)}};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)\right]$ in a buffer, so that we only need to compute $D(\theta^{k};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)$ in future iteration $k$ to construct $\widehat{\Delta}^{k,k^{(\ell)}}$ . Drawing sample from $\pi_{\theta^{k}}$ requires $T$ iterative score network calls by Equation 1, while computing $D(\theta^{k};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)$ only requires one. Hence, our method reduces much sampling cost. We plug $\exp(\widehat{\Delta}^{k, k^{(\ell)}})$ back to Equation 8 to enable reusing opponent buffers $\Pi^{-i,k}$ .

### 3.4 Self-Action Importance Sampling Stabilizes Training

*Figure 3: We use PCA to visualize the self-action buffer at iteration $101$ for Cournot $d=30$ .*

Recall evaluating the OMD loss Equation 7 requires samples from a player’s self action $\pi^{i,k}$ . Since we are maintaining replay buffers for both players, we can also use replay samples for a player’s own action, not just opponent action. Denote a player’s self action batch $\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{self}}$ . Instead of always getting fresh samples from $\pi^{i,k}$ , we use $\left\lceil\zeta|B_{\mathrm{self}}|\right\rceil$ IS samples with the rest from $\pi^{i,k}$ . Similar to opponent buffer reuse, we use the IS weight to correct distribution shift induced by replay samples. We defer the full algorithm details to Appendix C.

We find that adding importance-weighted replay stabilizes training and prevents premature plateaus. The policy starts concentrate on a narrow set of high-utility actions as it approaches equilibrium, limiting the coverage of fresh samples. Replaying diverse past actions broadens the training distribution and prevents the policy from overfitting to a narrow region. We visualize the impact of replay mechanism in Figure 3, where self action IS significantly improves coverage. We introduce an additional hyperparameter called trigger $\kappa$ , and we initialize the self-action IS once standard deviation of $\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{self}}$ falls below a fraction $\kappa$ of its initial value. We analyze the impact of the self action IS mechanism in Section 5.3.

## 4 Related Work

Equilibrium Computation. We provide a comprehensive review in Appendix B and focus here on learning-based approaches for continuous action spaces. Prior work learns generative approximate best responses (Kamra et al., 2019), trains randomized policy networks with zeroth-order equilibrium dynamics (Martin and Sandholm, 2023), or minimizes exploitability using learned best responses (Martin and Sandholm, 2025). In contrast, we parameterize each player’s evolving mixed strategy with a diffusion model to capture more expressive distributions.

Diffusion Models And Its Application in Online RL Diffusion models learn complex, multimodal distributions through iterative denoising and score matching (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021). Their ability to model complex distributions motivated their use as policy parameterizations in RL (Wang et al., 2024; Psenka et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025). Most closely related to ours, Ma et al. (2025) show that exponential reweighting of samples from the current diffusion policy is sufficient to implement a KL-regularized policy-improvement step. We adapt the reweighting technique and address it in the equilibrium computation setting. We give a comprehensive review of the field in Appendix B.

Diffusion Applications in Strategic Environment To our knowledge, the only direct application of diffusion to our setting is Karthikeyan and Pant (2025), which we include as a baseline and discuss in Section 5. We discuss diffusion model applications in other related strategic settings in Appendix B.

## 5 Experiments

Beyond the Cournot game, we evaluate DiffNash on a forest security game and a continuous variant of Colonel Blotto, two widely studied games that also admit intuitive visualizations.

Metrics and Baselines: We use Nash Gap (Definition 2) as our main evaluation metric. The best response optimization required in Nash Gap cannot be computed exactly. Following Kamra et al. (2019), we use an evolutionary search that repeatedly retains high-utility candidates and perturbs them with Gaussian noise to approximate the Nash Gap. We defer computation details to Section D.1.

We compare against three baselines. DeepFP (Kamra et al., 2019) represents each player’s strategy in FP with a neural generator $\mathcal{T}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})$ , where $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$ . Neural OMD adapts the mirror descent policy optimization framework of Tomar et al. (2022) to equilibrium computation, using a Gaussian neural policy for each player. DiffFP (Karthikeyan and Pant, 2025) parameterizes player strategies with diffusion models within FP. Since FP updates do not directly provide samples from the target strategy, DiffFP instead refines sampled actions $\mathbf{a}^{i}$ toward higher-utility regions using $\nabla_{\mathbf{a}^{i}}u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i};\Pi^{-i,k})$ and trains the diffusion policy on the refined actions. These baselines help isolate the benefits of diffusion policy and principled policy updates. For fair comparison, we train each player’s policy for $40K$ gradient updates across experiments. We use default hyperparameters for baselines.

### 5.1 Forest Security Game

Forest security game (Johnson et al., 2012) originated from forest economics (Albers, 2010). We consider the continuous version studied by Kamra et al. (2018) and DeepFP (Kamra et al., 2019). A defender selects $M$ locations to patrol, while an attacker selects $N$ locations to target in an endangered circular forest. Each location is parameterized by its radial distance and radian angle. Hence, defender and attacker’s action dimensionality are $2M$ and $2N$ , respectively. As $M$ and $N$ increase, the resulting strategy space becomes high-dimensional, a setting where Kamra et al. (2019) reports degraded performance. An attacker can collect trees within $R_{A}$ of its location, and a defender can stop any attacker within $R_{D}$ of them. The attacker’s utility is the value of the harvested trees but receives no value and incurs a penalty if caught by any defender. The defender’s utility is the negative of the attacker’s utility. Across experiments, we keep the interaction and payoff structure fixed and vary only the spatial distribution of trees along with the number of defenders and attackers. Changing the geometry creates qualitatively different optimal strategies by altering which attack locations are valuable, which regions can be protected together, and how many spatially separated patches the strategy must cover. In this game, we aim to find a robust patrol strategy for defender, so besides Nash gap, we also compute $\mathrm{Exploit_{D}}$ , measured as the attacker’s best-response reward against the learned average defender. We seek strategies profiles with low $\mathrm{Exploit_{D}}$ and Low Nash Gap $\mathrm{GAP}$ .

Experimental results. Table 1 shows that DiffNash achieves the best mean performance across all six forests, reducing Nash gap by an average of 35.6% relative to the strongest baseline. The gap is most pronounced in heterogeneous, multi-resource settings, where equilibrium strategies must distribute probability mass across several strategically distinct regions. DiffNash also achieves broader effective coverage. In F3 of Figure 4, for example, DiffNash’s guards (blue) concentrate around all four tree clusters (green), whereas DeepFP and DiffFP learn more diffuse patrol strategies and Neural OMD places substantial mass in low-tree-density regions. Importantly, diffuse coverage is not necessarily effective coverage: allocating guard probability to regions with few or no trees provides little protection value. We analyze the failure modes of all baselines:

- • DeepFP/NeuralOMD: Both exhibit mode collapse. In F2 of Figure 4, Neural OMD concentrates on a single forest patch. For DeepFP, Figure 4 and additional Appendix F.1 visualizations show both players’ strategies forming narrow circular bands. Since actions are represented in polar coordinates, this pattern indicates collapse along the radial dimension.

- • DiffFP: In large forests, small changes in guard locations are unlikely to change whether attackers are captured. Consequently, the defender utility gradient, i.e., $\nabla_{\mathbf{a}^{i}}u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i};\Pi^{-i,k})$ , is nearly zero for most locations, causing DiffFP’s defender strategy to get stuck, as shown by Figure 4’s F2. In contrast, DiffNash does not rely on local utility gradients. We update the entire defender policy in a principled way, yielding substantially better performance.

### 5.2 Continuous Colonel Blotto

Because allocations are coupled by the budget constraint, equilibrium play generally requires nontrivial randomization over a continuous action space. We consider games with $n=6$ and $n=10$ . ### 5.3 Ablation and Hyperparameter Study

Ablation We ablate the two importance-sampling components of DiffNash on Cournot ( $d=30$ ). In Figure 6, the green and blue curves almost overlap, indicating that opponent IS has little effect on convergence. Its primary benefit is computational: in this experiment, opponent IS reduces the number of score-network calls to roughly $66\%$ of that required without opponent IS. Moreover, DiffNash (orange) achieves the lowest Nash Gap, showing that self action IS prevents the early plateau observed without self action IS and reduces variance across runs. We observe a similar pattern in the forest ablation in Appendix F.4. These results support using IS for both opponent and self-action replay.

We additionally show our method’s performance in a general sum version of the Forest game in Section F.3.

Hyperparameter Study We provide hyperparameter study for self action IS ratio $\zeta$ , trigger $\kappa$ , self action buffer size and opponent action buffer size in Appendix F.5.

## 6 Conclusion

We develop DiffNash, a framework that parameterizes player strategies with diffusion models within OMD to compute Nash equilibria in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. We derive a reweighted score-matching objective that trains the diffusion model to realize OMD updates. To improve sample efficiency and training stability, we reuse past actions through a replay buffer and correct the resulting distribution shift with an ELBO-based importance-sampling strategy. On forest security and continuous Colonel Blotto games, DiffNash better recovers equilibrium distributions and reduces Nash gap by 35.6% and 24.7% compared to strongest baselines, respectively.

## Appendix A Limitations

We focus on two-player normal-form games. Extending DiffNash to multiplayer or sequential settings, is a natural direction for future work.

## Appendix B Additional Related Work

Equilibrium Computation Finite two-player zero-sum games admit linear-programming formulations [Dantzig, 1951], while equilibrium computation in finite general-sum games is PPAD-complete [Chen et al., 2009]. Continuous action games remain challenging because mixed strategies are distributions over infinite action spaces and best-response computation may require difficult continuous optimizaition. Prior work establishes continuous-action variants of fictitious-play [Perkins and Leslie, 2014] and develops strategy-generaion methods for zero-sum and general-sum continuous games [Adam et al., 2021, Kroupa and Votroubek, 2022]. Learning-based approaches include DeepFP, which learns generative approximate best responses [Kamra et al., 2019], randomized policy networks trained with zeroth-order equilibrium dynamics [Martin and Sandholm, 2023], and exploitability minimization with learned best responses [Martin and Sandholm, 2025] . Our approach instead parameterizes each player’s evolving mixed strategy with a diffusion model and trains it using FP and OMD based equilibrium updates [Rakhlin and Sridharan, 2013].

Diffusion and Flow-Based Models for Online RL Diffusion and flow-based policies have been widely studied for RL [Wang et al., 2024, Psenka et al., 2024, Ma et al., 2025, Ren et al., 2025]. Most closely related to our policy update, Ma et al. [2025] show that exponential reweighting of samples from the current diffusion policy implements a KL-regularized policy-improvement step, yielding Diffusion Policy Mirror Descent.

Related work also applies expressive diffusion policies in cooperative multi-agent RL [Li et al., 2026], while flow-matching policies have been developed for online continuous and combinatorial control [Park et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025, McAllister et al., 2026, Kong et al., 2026a]. These methods optimize return or coordination rather than equilibrium against strategic opponents. In our setting, policy-improvement weights depend on utility against an evolving opponent. We additionally use ELBO differences as approximate density ratios to reuse samples across strategic iterates.

#### Diffusion Applications in Strategic Environment

Diffusion models and their variants, such as flow matching [Lipman et al., 2023], have been applied to strategic settings adjacent to equilibrium computation. For auction theory, Wang et al. [2026] uses flow matching to represent bundle distributions in combinatorial auctions, achieving higher revenue while scaling to larger numbers of items. For green security game, when opponent data is available, diffusion and flow-based models can also be used to learn opponent behavior. Kong et al. [2025] uses diffusion models to learn poacher behavior in green security games and design robust patrol strategies. Kong et al. [2026b] uses flow matching to model poacher behavior from real-world data, and Kong et al. [2026c] subsequently uses reinforcement learning to plan patrol policies against the learned poacher behavioral model. Unlike these works, we assume no prior knowledge of opponent behavior and instead seek a Nash strategy, which provides a worst-case guarantee in 2p0s games.

We provide the full pseudocode for DiffNash in Algorithm 3. Algorithm 1 constructs replay entries, Algorithm 2 computes their ELBO-based importance weights, and Algorithm 3 gives the complete OMD training procedure. Self-action replay is activated only if the specified trigger fires; otherwise, training continues using fresh self-actions.

$$ t\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T\},\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). $$

## Appendix D Details about Experiment Setup

### D.1 Nash Gap Computation

For a learned strategy profile $\pi=(\pi^{1},\pi^{2})$ , we measure the total gain available from unilateral deviations. For player $i$ , define

$$ \epsilon^{i}(\pi)=\max_{a^{i}\in\mathcal{A}^{i}}u^{i}(a^{i};\pi^{-i})-U^{i}(\pi^{i},\pi^{-i}), $$

and compute the Nash gap as

$$ G(\pi^{1},\pi^{2})=\epsilon^{1}(\pi)+\epsilon^{2}(\pi). $$

Because expected utility is linear in the deviating strategy, it is sufficient to optimize over pure best responses. In the two-player zero-sum setting, writing $U$ for player 1’s payoff, this simplifies to

$$ G(\pi^{1},\pi^{2})=\max_{a^{1}\in\mathcal{A}^{1}}U(a^{1},\pi^{2})-\min_{a^{2}\in\mathcal{A}^{2}}U(\pi^{1},a^{2}). $$

For continuous action spaces, the best-response optimization is computed with a game-specific evaluation oracle. For the forest game, following Kamra et al. [2019], we use evolutionary search with a population of 50 candidates for 20 iterations. At each iteration, the top 10 candidates are retained and four Gaussian-perturbed mutations are generated from each survivor. Candidate utilities are estimated against 100 opponent samples during the search, and the resulting best response is reevaluated against 1,000 samples. When estimating the individual unilateral gains in (10), the utility of the learned profile is estimated from 2,000 sampled action pairs.

For symmetric Colonel Blotto, we follow the discretized best-response procedure of Adam et al. [2021]. Final Nash gaps use a simplex grid with spacing $1/1024$ and an exact knapsack dynamic program, with 20,000 samples from each learned policy. For the radial-band variant, we approximate each best response from a pool of approximately 11,400 candidates, refine the best 64 candidates for 400 gradient steps, and estimate final payoffs using 8,000 policy samples per player. The same evaluation procedure is used for all methods within each game.

### D.2 Experimental Details of Cournot Game

We consider a two-player multi-market Cournot competition game with $d$ independent markets, where $A>0$ is the demand intercept and $b>0$ controls the slope of inverse demand. Player $i\in\{1,2\}$ chooses production quantities across $d$ markets:

$$ \mathbf{a}^{i}=([\mathbf{a}^{i}]_{1},\ldots,[\mathbf{a}^{i}]_{d})\in[0,q_{\max}]^{d}. $$

In each market $j$ , the inverse demand function is

$$ p_{j}(\mathbf{a}^{1}_{j},\mathbf{a}^{2}_{j})=A-b(\mathbf{a}^{1}_{j}+\mathbf{a}^{2}_{j}), $$

and both firms have constant marginal cost $c$ . Player $i$ ’s total utility is

$$ u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i},\mathbf{a}^{-i})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left(A-b(\mathbf{a}^{i}_{j}+\mathbf{a}^{-i}_{j})-c\right)\mathbf{a}^{i}_{j}. $$

We use $A=10$ , $b=1$ , $c=1$ , and $q_{\max}=(A-c)/b=9$ , with $d\in\{1,30\}$ in the experiments.

In the implementation, the policy produces a normalized action $\mathbf{z}^{i}\in[-1,1]^{d}$ , which is mapped to the feasible Cournot action by

$$ \mathbf{a}^{i}=\frac{\mathbf{z}^{i}+1}{2}q_{\max}. $$

During optimization, we use the scaled utility $u^{i}/d$ so that its magnitude does not grow with the number of markets.

#### Analytical equilibrium.

The separability and quadratic structure of the Cournot game allow its Nash equilibrium to be characterized exactly.

#### Proposition 3.

The Cournot game in (12) has a unique Nash equilibrium $(\mathbf{a}^{1,\star},\mathbf{a}^{2,\star})$ , and for every market $j=1,\ldots,d$ ,

$$ [\mathbf{a}^{1,\star}]_{j}=[\mathbf{a}^{2,\star}]_{j}=\frac{A-c}{3b}. $$

Under our parameters, $[\mathbf{a}^{1,\star}]_{j}=[\mathbf{a}^{2,\star}]_{j}=3$ for every market.

#### Proof.

Consider an arbitrary mixed strategy $\pi^{-i}$ of player $-i$ , and let

$$ \mu^{-i}_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}^{-i}\sim\pi^{-i}}[[\mathbf{a}^{-i}]_{j}] $$

denote its mean production in market $j$ . Since the payoff is separable across markets and linear in the opponent’s production, the expected utility from a action $\mathbf{a}^{i}$ is

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}^{-i}\sim\pi^{-i}}\left[u^{i}(\mathbf{a}^{i},\mathbf{a}^{-i})\right]=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[(A-c-b\mu^{-i}_{j})\mathbf{a}^{i}_{j}-b(\mathbf{a}^{i}_{j})^{2}\right]. $$

For $b>0$ , this expression is strictly concave in $\mathbf{a}^{i}$ , so player $i$ has a unique best response against any mixed opponent strategy. In each market,

$$ \operatorname{BR}^{i}_{j}(\pi^{-i})=\frac{A-c-b\mu^{-i}_{j}}{2b}. $$

Since

$$ 0\leq\mu^{-i}_{j}\leq q_{\max}=\frac{A-c}{b}, $$

this quantity lies in $[0,q_{\max}]$ , so the action constraints do not alter the best response.

A player can randomize at a Nash equilibrium only over best responses. Since the best response is unique, every Nash equilibrium must therefore be pure (all probability mass on a single action). For each market $j$ , the equilibrium quantities satisfy

$$ 2b[\mathbf{a}^{1,\star}]_{j}+b[\mathbf{a}^{2,\star}]_{j}=A-c,\qquad b[\mathbf{a}^{1,\star}]_{j}+2b[\mathbf{a}^{2,\star}]_{j}=A-c. $$

Subtracting the two equations gives $[\mathbf{a}^{1,\star}]_{j}=[\mathbf{a}^{2,\star}]_{j}$ , and substitution yields

$$ [\mathbf{a}^{1,\star}]_{j}=[\mathbf{a}^{2,\star}]_{j}=\frac{A-c}{3b}. $$

Because the markets are independent, this holds for every $j=1,\ldots,d$ . With $A=10$ , $b=1$ , and $c=1$ , the equilibrium quantity is $3$ in every market. ∎

### D.3 Experimental Details of Forest Protection Game

#### D.3.1 Environment Details

We use the continuous forest security game introduced by Kamra et al. [2018] and subsequently adopted as the forest protection benchmark in DeepFP [Kamra et al., 2019]. Our environment and parameter settings follow the latter. The game is played between a defender $D$ and an adversary $A$ in a circular forest containing a fixed set of tree locations $\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . The adversary controls $N$ adversaries, while the defender controls $M$ stationary guards.

Each adversary enters at the boundary of the forest, travels along a radial path toward the center, stops at a chosen location, and exits along the same path. Its stopping location therefore determines both its trajectory and its harvesting region. The adversary’s action is

$$ \mathbf{a}_{A}=([\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{1},\ldots,[\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{N})\in\mathcal{F}^{N}, $$

where $\mathcal{F}$ is the unit disk and $[\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{k}$ is the stopping location of the $k$ -th adversary. The defender selects the guard locations

$$ \mathbf{a}_{D}=([\mathbf{a}_{D}]_{1},\ldots,[\mathbf{a}_{D}]_{M})\in\mathcal{F}^{M}. $$

where $[\mathbf{a}_{D}]_{j}$ is the location of guard $j$ . Locations are represented using normalized polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ , so the adversary and defender action dimensions are $2N$ and $2M$ , respectively.

An adversary is captured when its path passes within guard radius $R_{g}$ of at least one defender resource. Let $P_{k}([\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{k})$ denote the radial path followed by the adversary $k$ . Its capture indicator is

$$ C_{k}(\mathbf{a}_{D},\mathbf{a}_{A})=\mathbb{I}\left[\min_{j\in\{1,\ldots,M\}}\min_{p\in P_{k}([\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{k})}\lVert p-[\mathbf{a}_{D}]_{j}\rVert_{2}\leq R_{D}\right]. $$

An uncaptured adversary harvests trees lying within chopping radius $R_{A}$ of its stopping location. Define

$$ H_{k}([\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{k})=\left\{t\in\mathcal{T}:\lVert t-[\mathbf{a}_{A}]_{k}\rVert_{2}\leq R_{A}\right\}. $$

Let $N_{\mathrm{stolen}}(\mathbf{a}_{D},\mathbf{a}_{A})$ denote the number of trees successfully removed by the uncaptured adversaries, with overlapping harvest regions combined according to the game simulator. A captured adversary loses its harvest and incurs a penalty $r_{\mathrm{pen}}>0$ . The adversary’s reward is

$$ u_{A}(a_{D},a_{A})=N_{\mathrm{stolen}}(a_{D},a_{A})-r_{\mathrm{pen}}\sum_{k=1}^{N}C_{k}(a_{D},a_{A}), $$

and the defender receives the negative reward, $u_{D}(a_{D},a_{A})=-u_{A}(a_{D},a_{A})$ . Following the DeepFP experimental setup [Kamra et al., 2019], we use

$$ R_{D}=0.1,\qquad R_{A}=0.04,\qquad r_{\mathrm{pen}}=4.0. $$

The reward landscape is highly nonconvex and contains large flat regions. In particular, moving a guard without changing which trajectories it intercepts does not change the defender’s reward. Heterogeneous tree densities also create spatially separated high-value regions, so effective mixed strategies may place probability mass on several distinct guard or adversary configurations. The game therefore tests both the expressiveness of the learned strategy distribution and its ability to improve when informative utility gradients are sparse.

#### Forest instances.

We use four forest layouts, denoted F1–F4 throughout the paper. F1 and F2 contain 4,000 and 6,000 trees, respectively, and are evaluated with $M=N\in\{1,3\}$ . F3 and F4 are denser layouts containing 6,200 and 7,100 trees and are evaluated with $M=N=5$ . Thus, the six configurations reported in the main experiments are

$$ (\mathrm{F1},1),\;(\mathrm{F1},3),\;(\mathrm{F2},1),\;(\mathrm{F2},3),\;(\mathrm{F3},5),\;(\mathrm{F4},5). $$

The interaction and payoff structure is held fixed across instances; only the spatial tree layout and number of resources change. This changes which attack locations are valuable and how many spatially separated regions must be represented by the equilibrium strategy.

#### Scaling the action space.

Each guard and adversary is represented by a polar coordinate $(r,\theta)$ , so the defender and attacker action spaces have dimensions $2M$ and $2N$ , respectively. Latent actions in $[-1,1]$ are mapped to $r\in[0,1]$ and $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$ . Consequently, the headline experiments increase each player’s action dimension from 2 at $M=N=1$ , to 6 at $M=N=3$ , and 10 at $M=N=5$ . Although resources of the same type are interchangeable in the payoff, we use the direct ordered representation and do not explicitly enforce permutation symmetry.

#### D.3.2 Implementation Details

#### Compared methods.

We compare DiffNash with DeepFP [Kamra et al., 2019], DiffFP [Karthikeyan and Pant, 2025], and Neural OMD. DeepFP uses neural fictitious play with a learned attacker and geometric defender best response. DiffFP replaces the neural policy with a diffusion best response while retaining fictitious-play updates. Neural OMD uses the same OMD training loop as DiffNash but represents the policy with a squashed diagonal Gaussian, isolating the contribution of the diffusion policy. DiffNash combines a diffusion policy with OMD, opponent replay, and self-action importance sampling.

#### Training details.

All headline methods are trained for 40,000 gradient updates per player. DiffNash and Neural OMD use 2,000 outer OMD iterations with 20 inner updates per iteration. DiffFP uses 100 fictitious-play iterations with 400 best-response updates per iteration. Unless otherwise noted, we run five seeds. OMD methods use batches of 256 player actions and 128 opponent replay samples. DiffNash maintains a FIFO opponent replay buffer of size 1,024 and draws 1% of each player batch from its full self-action history.

DiffNash and Neural OMD use Adam Kingma and Ba [2014] with learning rate $3\times 10^{-4}$ , decayed to $3\times 10^{-5}$ during training. The diffusion policies use $T=20$ denoising steps. All experiments are run on CPU using 8 cores and 16 GB of memory.

#### Evaluation.

We report defender exploitability, defined as the best attacker reward against the learned time-averaged defender, together with the two sided Nash gap. Best responses are approximated using evolutionary search on the reference simulator. The search uses a population of 50 candidates for 20 iterations, retaining the top 10 and generating four mutations per survivor. Each candidate is evaluated against 100 sampled opponent actions, followed by a final evaluation against 1,000 samples. Self-play utility for the Nash gap is estimated from 2,000 sampled action pairs.

We evaluate only the final checkpoint and use the complete time-averaged strategy accumulated during training. Reported uncertainty is the 95% Student- $t$ confidence interval across seeds.

#### Hyperparameters.

DiffNash uses a DACER-style denoiser with three 256-unit hidden layers and Mish activations. The diffusion-time embedding is a 16-dimensional sinusoidal encoding followed by a two-layer MLP. We use OMD step size $\eta=1$ , normalize utility-derived energies within each batch, clip their logits to $[-3,3]$ , and renormalize the resulting weights to mean one. Opponent importance ratios are upper-clipped at 10. Self-action replay constitutes 1% of the training batch and is activated once the standard deviation of the current action samples falls below 10% of its initial value.

### D.4 Experimental Details of Continuous Colonel Blotto

#### D.4.1 Environment Details

We follow the continuous Colonel Blotto formulation of Adam et al. [2021]. Two players simultaneously allocate a unit budget across $N$ battlefields. Both players have the action space

$$ \mathcal{A}^{1}=\mathcal{A}^{2}=\mathcal{A}=\left\{\mathbf{a}=([\mathbf{a}]_{1},\ldots,[\mathbf{a}]_{N})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}:\sum_{j=1}^{N}[\mathbf{a}]_{j}=1\right\}. $$

Let $\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2}\in\mathcal{A}$ denote the allocations selected by players $1$ and $2$ , respectively. The symmetric case and radial band case of Table 2 differ in the utility function of the agent, which we detail below.

#### Symmetric

To construct the symmetric case of Table 2, we define the following battlefield contest function:

$$ \ell_{c}(z)=\begin{cases}-1,&z\leq-c,\\[2.84526pt]
z/c,&-c<z<c,\\[2.84526pt]
1,&z\geq c,\end{cases} $$

, where $\omega_{j}$ is battlefield $j$ ’s positive weight and $c>0$ controls the allocation advantage required to obtain the full value of a battlefield. Player $1$ ’s utility is

$$ u^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\omega_{j}\,\ell_{c}(\mathbf{a}^{1}_{j}-\mathbf{a}^{2}_{j}), $$

and player $2$ receives

$$ u^{2}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})=-u^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2}). $$

Thus, player $1$ receives $\omega_{j}$ when it allocates at least $c$ more than player $2$ to battlefield $j$ , receives $-\omega_{j}$ when it allocates at least $c$ less, and receives a payoff that varies linearly with the allocation difference inside this margin. Our symmetric Blotto experiment uses the symmetric N-battlefield setting

$$ \omega_{j}=1\ \text{for all }j,\qquad c=\frac{1}{16}. $$

for $N=\{6,10\}$ . As $c\rightarrow 0$ , $\ell_{c}$ approaches the sign function used in the classical continuous Colonel Blotto game.

The game is symmetric and zero-sum, so its equilibrium value is zero. Because the budget constraint couples all six coordinates, increasing the allocation to one battlefield reduces the allocation available to the others. Equilibrium play therefore requires coordinated allocations rather than independent decisions at individual battlefields. This makes the game a useful test of whether a policy class can represent a broad mixed strategy.

#### Radial-band instances.

To construct the radial band case of Table 2, we first specify precisely what the radial band is. Define the uniform allocation $\bar{\mathbf{a}}$ which allocates $\frac{1}{N}$ budget to each battlefield, and define $\mathbf{e}_{1}$ be the allocation which allocates all battles to the first battlefield. Now define: $v_{\mathrm{rad}}=\mathbf{e}_{1}-\bar{\mathbf{a}}$ , center line $\gamma_{\mathrm{rad}}(\tau)=\bar{\mathbf{a}}+\tau v_{\mathrm{rad}}$ , and width $\omega_{\mathrm{rad}}(\tau)=\min\{0.06,0.20(1-\tau)\}$ . The radial interval is $[\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}]$ , with

$$ \tau_{\min}=\begin{cases}0.12,&n=6,\\
0.15,&n=10,\end{cases} $$

and $\tau_{\max}=0.995$ . $\gamma_{\mathrm{rad}}(\tau)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{rad}}(\tau)$ together define the shape of the radial band.

The next step we define how probability is distributed within the band. We put $60\%$ of the probability along the interior portion and $40\%$ closer to the vertex. To achieve that we first sample First sample

$$ \tau\sim\begin{cases}\operatorname{Unif}[\tau_{\min},0.80),&\text{with probability }0.6,\\
\operatorname{Unif}[0.80,\tau_{\max}],&\text{with probability }0.4.\end{cases} $$

We also add some perpendicular displacement to make the distribution has width. Formally, given $\tau$ , draw the displacement $\xi$ uniformly from

$$ \left\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\mathbf{1}^{\top}\xi=0,\quad v_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\top}\xi=0,\quad\|\xi\|_{2}\leq w_{\mathrm{rad}}(\tau),\quad\gamma_{\mathrm{rad}}(\tau)+\xi\in\Delta^{N-1}\right\}. $$

The first constraint make sure the resulting allocation does not exceed the budget, and the second make sure the displacement is orthogonal to the radial band. Define the target distribution $\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}$ as the law of $\gamma_{\mathrm{rad}}+\xi$ .

Before we specify the payoff which makes $\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}$ the equilibrium strategy, we first define the following notations. For any allocation, we first locate its clipped projection onto the centerline, measure its perpendicular distance, and finally penalize the portion that exceeds the allowed width. Define the projected radial coordinate $\widehat{\tau}(\mathbf{a})$ and penalty $V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a})$ by

$$ \widehat{\tau}(\mathbf{a})=\min\left\{\tau_{\max},\max\left\{\tau_{\min},\frac{\langle\mathbf{a}-\bar{\mathbf{a}},\,v_{\mathrm{rad}}\rangle}{\|v_{\mathrm{rad}}\|_{2}^{2}}\right\}\right\}, $$

$$ V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a})=-15\left[\left\|\mathbf{a}-\gamma_{\mathrm{rad}}\bigl(\widehat{\tau}(\mathbf{a})\bigr)\right\|_{2}-w_{\mathrm{rad}}\bigl(\widehat{\tau}(\mathbf{a})\bigr)\right]_{+}. $$

Here $V_{\mathrm{rad}}\leq 0$ , and every target sample does not receive penalty. We also define the following Gaussian kernel $K(\cdot,\cdot)$ which measure the similarity between allocations:

$$ K(a^{1},a^{2})=\exp\left(-\frac{\|a^{1}-a^{2}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma_{K}^{2}}\right). $$

, with bandwidth $\sigma_{K}=0.08$ . We define a centered version of the Gaussian kernel where we subtract each allocation’s average similarity to the target radial shape $\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}$ , then add back the target’s average similarity to itself. Formally, for independent samples $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{b}^{\prime}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}$ , define

$$ \bar{K}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})=K(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}}K(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{b})-\mathbb{E}_{b}K(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{a}^{2})+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b},\mathbf{b}^{\prime}}K(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{b}^{\prime}). $$

Set player $1$ ’s utilities to $u^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})=\bar{K}_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})+V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a}^{1})-V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a}^{2})$ and set $u^{2}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})=-u^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2})$ .

#### Proposition 4 (Radial Band is a Nash equilibrium).

$(\mu_{\mathrm{rad}},\mu_{\mathrm{rad}})$ is the Nash equilibrium of the game we described above.

#### Proof.

Observe that for every $\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2}\in\Delta^{N-1}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}}\left[\bar{K}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{b})\right]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}}\left[\bar{K}(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{a}^{2})\right]=0, $$

by the definition of the centered kernel. Since $\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is supported inside the corridor, $V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{b})=0$ almost surely for $\mathbf{b}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}$ , while $V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a})\leq 0$ for every feasible action.

Let $U^{1}$ denote the expected utility induced by $u^{1}$ . For any pure deviations $\mathbf{a}^{1}$ and $\mathbf{a}^{2}$ , we therefore have

$$ U^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mu_{\mathrm{rad}})=V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a}^{1})\leq 0,\qquad U^{1}(\mu_{\mathrm{rad}},\mathbf{a}^{2})=-V_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{a}^{2})\geq 0. $$

Moreover,

$$ U^{1}(\mu_{\mathrm{rad}},\mu_{\mathrm{rad}})=0. $$

Thus,

$$ U^{1}(\mathbf{a}^{1},\mu_{\mathrm{rad}})\leq U^{1}(\mu_{\mathrm{rad}},\mu_{\mathrm{rad}})\leq U^{1}(\mu_{\mathrm{rad}},\mathbf{a}^{2}) $$

for all $\mathbf{a}^{1},\mathbf{a}^{2}\in\Delta^{n-1}$ . These inequalities extend to mixed deviations by linearity of expected utility. Hence $(\mu_{\mathrm{rad}},\mu_{\mathrm{rad}})$ is an exact Nash equilibrium with value zero for both $N=6$ and $N=10$ . ∎

In implementation, we replace $\mu_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\star}$ by a fixed empirical distribution and compute all kernel-centering terms from the same bank. The same argument then applies exactly to the resulting finite game.

#### Visualization.

For visualization, six-dimensional allocations are projected onto a regular hexagon using barycentric coordinates. Let $[\mathbf{a}]_{1},\ldots,[\mathbf{a}]_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ denote the hexagon vertices. An allocation $\mathbf{a}$ is plotted at

$$ p(\mathbf{a})=\sum_{j=1}^{N}[\mathbf{a}]_{j}e_{j}. $$

Under this projection, the uniform allocation appears at the hexagon center. Allocating the entire budget to battlefield $j$ would map directly to vertex $e_{j}$ . The same projection is used for both the standard Blotto and radial-band games, which allows their learned strategy distributions to be compared directly.

#### D.4.2 Implementation Details

#### Reference solutions.

For the symmetric Colonel Blotto instances, we compute reference equilibria with the grid-based double-oracle (DO) solver proposed in Adam et al. [2021]. For both $N=6$ and $N=10$ , we discretize allocations with grid spacing $1/256$ and run DO to tolerance $10^{-6}$ , using an exact knapsack dynamic program to compute best responses over the discretized action space. For $N=6$ , DO terminates after $21$ iterations with a $42$ -action support and Nash gap $4.31\times 10^{-14}$ ; for $N=10$ , it terminates after $12$ iterations with a $50$ -action support and gap $1.33\times 10^{-14}$ . Both instances use $c=1/16$ . This solver relies on a game-specific best-response oracle: discretization makes exact best responses tractable for these Blotto instances, but such an oracle is generally unavailable in high-dimensional continuous-action games, where best-response optimization may itself be difficult and uniform discretization scales poorly with dimension. We therefore use DO only to construct reference equilibria for these structured symmetric instances, rather than as a general-purpose baseline.

For the radial-band instances, the reference equilibrium is known by construction. We instantiate it using a fixed empirical distribution $\widehat{\mu}^{\star}_{n}$ with $K=1200$ anchors, consisting of $720$ samples from the interior portion of the corridor and $480$ from the near-extreme portion. The anchor bank is sampled once for each game instance and then frozen, and all kernel-centering terms are computed from the same bank. Thus, $\widehat{\mu}^{\star}_{n}$ is an exact equilibrium of the implemented finite-anchor game. We use $r_{\min}=0.12$ for $N=6$ and $r_{\min}=0.15$ for $N=10$ , with $r_{\mathrm{split}}=0.80$ and $r_{\max}=0.995$ . The corresponding reference Nash gap is exactly zero. We additionally report the finite-sample evaluation floors, $0.014213$ for $N=6$ and $0.024741$ for $N=10$ .

#### Compared Methods.

We compare DiffNash against DeepFP, DiffFP, and Neural OMD. For DeepFP, we use the original implementation provided by the authors; their codebase is not publicly released. For DiffFP, no implementation is available, so we reimplement the method from the paper, using diffusion policies within the fictitious-play update and its $Q$ -guided action refinement procedure.

We additionally introduce Neural OMD as a controlled baseline to separate the effect of the OMD update from the expressive diffusion used by DiffNash. Neural OMD uses the same OMD training structure and optimization budget as DiffNash, but replaces the diffusion policy with a squashed diagonal-Gaussian policy parameterized by a two-layer MLP with hidden dimensions $(256,256)$ and tanh activations. Because this policy admits a tractable density, the mirror-descent regularizer is implemented using the analytic KL divergence between consecutive policies, with coefficient $1.0$ . Neural OMD is trained on-policy using fresh samples at each outer iteration and doe not use a replay buffer for importance weighting.

For a given seed, all methods are evaluated on the same game instance and frozen anchor bank. The target distribution, kernel centering terms, and payoff parameters are therefore identical across methods.

#### Training details.

All four experiments use five random seeds $0$ - $4$ .

DiffNash and Neural OMD each use $2000$ outer iterations with $20$ gradient updates per iteration, for a total of $40,000$ updates per player. Both use Adam with a learning rate annealed from $3\times 10^{-4}$ to $3\times 10^{-5}$ , a policy batch size of $256$ , and $128$ opponent samples. DiffNash parameterizes each policy with a $20$ -step diffusion model with three hidden layers of width $256$ and a linear noise schedule scaled by 0.8. Its replay buffer if FIFO with capacity $1024$ , with $32$ new samples added per outer iteration. Opponent samples are corrected using importance weights capped at $10$ . For own-policy correction, $3$ of the $256$ samples in each batch are importance weighted, corresponding to approximately $1.17\%$ of the batch.

DiffFP uses a $20$ -step diffusion model with hidden dimensions $(256,256)$ and a $32$ -dimensional time embedding. We train it for $100$ fictitious-play iterations, with $400$ best-response updates per iteration, again giving $40{,}000$ gradient updates. It uses Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2014] with learning rate $3\times 10^{-4}$ , gradient-norm clipping at $2.0$ , training batches of $256$ , and rollout batches of $32$ . Its replay buffer has capacity $200{,}000$ , with a pool of $100$ historical policies, and the best-response policy is reinitialized at each fictitious-play iteration. DiffFP does not use importance sampling.

DeepFP uses the authors’ TensorFlow 1 implementation, with a two-layer $(128,128)$ policy network followed by a softmax output. We use Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$ and train for $400{,}000$ games, applying a policy update every $10$ games.

#### Evaluation

We measure convergence using the two-player zero-sum Nash gap

$$ G(p,q)=\max_{x}U(x,q)-\min_{y}U(p,y), $$

which is the sum of the two players’ unilateral improvement incentives and is zero at equilibrium.

For symmetric Blotto, we follow the double-oracle evaluation of Adam et al. [2021], computing best responses exactly on a discretized simplex with a knapsack dynamic program. Reference solutions use grid spacing $1/256$ , while final Nash gaps use a finer $1/1024$ grid and $20{,}000$ policy samples per player. For the radial-band games, we approximate each best response using a pool of approximately $11{,}400$ candidates followed by $400$ gradient-refinement steps on the best $64$ , and estimate payoffs using $8{,}000$ samples per player. We additionally report recovery of the known radial equilibrium, including near-extreme mass ( $0.40$ at equilibrium) and active versus inactive radial mass. All metrics are aggregated over five seeds using the same evaluator for every method within each game.

Under the forward process,

$$ \mathbf{a}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathbf{a}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). $$

We first express the reconstruction term and each denoising KL term as an expectation of $D(\theta;a_{0},t,\epsilon)$ , with additive constants independent of $\theta$ . $$ \displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{0}-\mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{1},1) \displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{a}_{1}-\sqrt{\beta_{1}}\epsilon-\mathbf{a}_{1}-\beta_{1}s_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{1},1)}{\sqrt{\alpha_{1}}} \displaystyle=-\frac{\beta_{1}}{\sqrt{\alpha_{1}}}\left(s_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{1},1)+\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{\beta_{1}}}\right). $$

For the Gaussian decoder $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0}\mid\mathbf{a}_{1})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}_{0};\mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{1},1),\sigma_{1}^{2}I)$ with fixed $\sigma_{1}^{2}>0$ , by plugging in 32, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{0}\mid\mathbf{a}_{1}) \displaystyle=-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_1^2)-\frac{\|\mathbf{a}_{0}-\mu_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{1},1)\|_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma_{1}^{2}} \displaystyle=-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_1^2)-\underbrace{\frac{\beta_{1}^{2}}{2\sigma_{1}^{2}\alpha_{1}}}_{C_{1}}\left\|s_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{1},1)+\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{1}}}\right\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_1^2)-D(\theta;\mathbf{a}_{0},1,\epsilon). $$

The coefficient $C_{1}$ has the same form as $C_{t}=\beta_{t}^{2}/(2\sigma_{t}^{2}\alpha_{t})$ for $t\geq 2$ .

#### Combining the Reconstruction Term and the denoising KL term

Because the two policy iterates share the same forward schedule, reverse-variance schedule, and terminal prior, the same $\mathrm{const}(\mathbf{a}_{0})$ applies to both. Consequently, the constant terms get cancelled and we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{ELBO}^{k}(\mathbf{a}_{0})-\operatorname{ELBO}^{k^{(\ell)}}(\mathbf{a}_{0}) \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\left[D(\theta^{k^{(\ell)}};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)-D(\theta^{k};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)\right]. $$

Finally, because $t\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,T\}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon}[\widehat{\Delta}^{k,k^{(\ell)}}] \displaystyle=T\,\mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon}\left[D(\theta^{k^{(\ell)}};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)-D(\theta^{k};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\left[D(\theta^{k^{(\ell)}};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)-D(\theta^{k};\mathbf{a}_{0},t,\epsilon)\right] \displaystyle=\operatorname{ELBO}^{k^{(\ell)}}(\mathbf{a}_{0})-\operatorname{ELBO}^{k}(\mathbf{a}_{0}). $$

Thus, $\widehat{\Delta}^{k,k^{(\ell)}}$ is an unbiased estimator of the ELBO difference. ∎

### F.3 General-Sum Forest Protection

We also consider a general-sum variant of the F2 forest protection game found in Kamra et al. [2019]. We retain the original F2 geometry and interaction mechanics, but assign each tree separate ecological and economic values. This creates different objectives for the defender and poacher without changing the continuous action space.

Let $v_{t}^{D}$ and $v_{t}^{P}$ denote the ecological and economic values of tree $t$ , respectively. For each adversary logger $l$ , let $a_{l}=1$ indicate that it is captured by at least one guard and let $s_{t,l}$ denote its share of tree $t$ when multiple adversary target the same tree. The payoffs are

$$ \displaystyle u^{D} \displaystyle=\sum_{l}\left[-(1-a_{l})\sum_{t}s_{t,l}v_{t}^{D}+4a_{l}\right], \displaystyle u^{P} \displaystyle=\sum_{l}\left[(1-a_{l})\sum_{t}s_{t,l}v_{t}^{P}-4a_{l}\right]. $$

where $a_{l}$ indicates whether adversary $l$ is captured and $s_{(t,l}$ is its share of tree $t$ . The original zero-sum game is recovered when $v_{t}^{D}=v_{t}^{P}=1$ .

We construct the two value fields to favor different parts of the forest. For a tree $t$ , let $r_{t}$ denote its radial distance from the center and let $k_{t}$ be the number of other trees within Euclidean distance $0.05$ . We define

$$ \widetilde{v}_{t}^{D}=\frac{\exp(-r_t/0.3)}{1+k_{t}},\qquad\widetilde{v}_{t}^{P}=\exp\left(-\frac{1-r_{t}}{0.3}\right)(1+k_{t}). $$

and independently rescale and clip each field to $[0.25,4]$ while preserving mean 1, so that the overall payoff scale is comparable to the original game. Thus, the defender places greater value on isolated interior trees, while the poacher focuses more on dense patches near the boundary. On F2, the two value fields have correlation $-0.52$ .

Neural OMD performs better than the FP-based methods, but exhibits higher variance than DiffNash. The visualized seed also shows qualitatively different spatial strategies across methods.

### F.4 Importance-sampling Forest ablation

*Figure 10: Importance-sampling ablation on F2. Removing own-policy importance sampling substantially degrades DiffNash, whereas opponent IS has little effect on convergence when own IS is omitted.*

We use F2, where $m=n=3$ , to isolate the roles of the two importance-sampling corrections in DiffNash. In particular, we separate the correction applied to replayed samples from the player’s own past policies (own IS) from the correction used when evaluating samples from past opponent policies (opponent IS). Figure 10 shows that the two corrections have different effects. Removing own IS substantially degrades performance, increasing the Nash gap from $300.7\pm 126.4$ for the full DiffNash method to $797.0\pm 153.4$ with opponent IS alone. In contrast, opponent IS has little effect on convergence when own IS is omitted: the Nash gap is $787.1\pm 134.6$ without either correction and $797.0\pm 153.4$ with opponent IS alone. This is consistent with the Cournot ablation in the main paper (Figure 6, where opponent IS likewise has little effect on convergence performance, but reduces score-network calls to roughly $66\%$ of those required without opponent IS. Together, these results suggest that own IS provides the primary optimization benefit by correcting the distribution shift induced by reusing the player’s historical diffusion samples, while opponent IS mainly improves computational efficiency.

### F.5 Forest Game Hyperparameter Sweep

We fix other hyperparamters and change self action rate $\zeta$ in Figure 11. Figure 11 shows that lower self-action IS rates generally yield smaller mean Nash gaps. Because importance weights are clipped, including too many samples from past iterations may bias the OMD loss in Equation 7. Empirically, a $1\%$ self-action IS rate suffices to stabilize training.
